title: The World's Most Thrilling Theme Parks and Rides
passages: What makes a roller coaster so EXHILARATING (thrilling, exciting, electrifying)? Thrill rides play clever tricks on your body using SPEED, HEIGHT, sudden DROPS, and the strange feeling of WEIGHTLESSNESS. As you race down a hill, your brain senses danger and floods your body with ADRENALINE, a HORMONE that makes your heart pound and your senses sharpen.

Here is the surprising part: most roller coasters have no ENGINE at all. A chain or LAUNCH system pulls the train up the very first hill, and after that, GRAVITY does almost all the work. Standing still on the ground, your body feels a normal PULL of just 1 G, but a thrilling ride can make that force feel many times STRONGER. That is why the first hill is usually the tallest, and the first drop is usually the most TERRIFYING (frightening, alarming, petrifying). The brief floating feeling you get over the top of a hill even has a name among fans: AIRTIME.

If you crave pure speed, no ride beats Formula Rossa at Ferrari World in ABU DHABI. Since 2010 it has held the record as the fastest roller coaster on Earth, ROCKETING (racing, speeding, hurtling) riders to an ASTONISHING 240 kilometres per hour in under five seconds. It ACCELERATES so RAPIDLY (quickly, swiftly, speedily) that it uses the same kind of powerful CATAPULT launch system found in fighter jets.

The ride is so fast that riders are actually REQUIRED to wear protective GOGGLES. Without them, tiny specks of desert SAND and dust would sting their EYES like little bullets at top speed. Reaching that VELOCITY in a heartbeat presses riders back into their seats with TREMENDOUS force.

For decades, the king of height was Kingda Ka at Six Flags Great Adventure in NEW JERSEY. When it opened in 2005, it became the tallest roller coaster in the world, BLASTING riders straight up a TOWER a DIZZYING 456 feet into the sky before dropping them back down. It was so ICONIC (famous, legendary, celebrated) that it stood UNMATCHED for years, until it was finally removed in 2024 to make way for an even bigger record-breaker.

Height is only half the story; STEEPNESS matters too. On a DIVE coaster, the train climbs to the top, then DANGLES (hangs, suspends, holds) riders over the edge for a few terrifying seconds before letting them fall. Some modern coasters even feature drops that are 'beyond VERTICAL', TILTING riders past straight down so it feels as though the track has DISAPPEARED beneath them.

Roller coasters may grab the headlines, but theme parks are where the MAGIC lives. The most visited theme park on Earth is Magic Kingdom at Walt Disney World in ORLANDO, Florida. It has been the world's most POPULAR (well-known, renowned, celebrated) park for nearly twenty years in a row, welcoming around 18 million VISITORS every single year. Its FAIRY-TALE symbol, CINDERELLA Castle, is one of the most PHOTOGRAPHED buildings on the planet.

Disney is far from alone, though. FAMOUS parks pull in HUGE crowds all around the GLOBE, including Disneyland in California, Tokyo Disneyland in Japan, and Europa-Park in Germany. Each one MIXES thrilling rides with shows, THEMED lands, and a sense of WONDER designed to DELIGHT visitors of every age.

Some roller coasters break records so ASTONISHING (amazing, staggering, incredible) they almost sound made up. The longest roller coaster in the world is Steel Dragon 2000 at Nagashima Spa Land in JAPAN, STRETCHING an INCREDIBLE 2,480 metres, longer than 24 football pitches laid end to end. Riding it from start to finish takes around four whole MINUTES.

Other coasters chase different records. The Smiler at Alton Towers in ENGLAND holds the world record for the most INVERSIONS, FLIPPING (turning, rolling, spinning) riders upside down a STOMACH-CHURNING 14 times in a single ride. Meanwhile, the OLDEST roller coaster still running today first opened over a hundred years ago, proving that the love of a good THRILL never really goes out of FASHION.

Why does a roller coaster feel so scary when it is actually very safe? The answer is G-FORCE, the force you feel as a ride speeds up, slows down, or WHIPS around a curve. It is measured in units called G. Standing still, you feel a normal 1 G. On an INTENSE (extreme, fierce, severe) coaster you might briefly feel 4 or 5 G, while fighter pilots can ENDURE forces of up to 9 G.

Of course, all that force would be DANGEROUS without careful DESIGN. ENGINEERS TEST every ride for years and lock riders in securely with strong RESTRAINTS, such as padded shoulder bars. They also build trains with POWERFUL BRAKES so that a coaster always halts exactly where it should. The thrill is real, but the danger is mostly an ILLUSION (trick, deception, mirage) created by clever SCIENCE.
